text: Capel is a town in the South West region of Western Australia, situated 212 kilometres (132 mi) south of Perth and halfway between Bunbury and Busselton. It lies on the Capel River and is approximately 19 metres (62 ft) above sea level. The area was originally inhabited by the Wardandi Noongar people. Colonists first visited the region during the early history of colonial Western Australia; the Capel River was explored by Frederick Ludlow in 1834, though it received an English name later, after the Bussell family settled there. The name Capel honours Capel Carter Brockman (1839–1924), daughter of John Bussell (1803–1875), who was named after Miss Capel Carter, a cousin of the Bussells in England with whom family members corresponded. In the 1830s, several settlers followed the Bussells into the area, and both James Stirling and John Hutt, the first two Governors of Western Australia, took up land there. Plans to establish a townsite were first discussed in 1844, but the site was not surveyed until the 1870s and lots were not sold until 1897. The town was initially named Coolingnup, the Noongar name for the location, and was renamed Capel in 1899. Capel has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate (Köppen: Csa), with Forrest Beach, at a certain distance from the town, having a warm-summer version (Csb), marking the northern boundary of that climatic zone in Australia. The town experiences hot dry summers and cool wet winters, with daily temperatures ranging from 13 °C to 40 °C in summer and from 5 °C to 27 °C in winter, and an average annual rainfall of about 830 mm. The population of the town was 91 (44 males and 47 females) in 1898. According to the 2016 census, the population of the Town of Capel was 2,509, and the population of the Shire of Capel was 17,123. Historically, Capel has been a farming area, with traditional agricultural activities including dairy and beef. Recently, it has gained popularity for hobby farms and has seen the introduction of innovative pursuits such as alpacas, viticulture, aquaculture, and blue gum cultivation. There is also some mining of mineral sands in the Shire, and tourism has become increasingly important to the Shire's economy. Westralian Sands was established in 1954 but began operations in 1959 at the Yoganup deposit just north of the town. Another company, RGC, operated a mine to the south of the town. In 1998, both companies merged to form Iluka Resources, which continues to operate ilmenite mines in the area and produces synthetic rutile at a processing facility located north of the town along the Bussell Highway.
